# Pitch script (about 2½ minutes)

*Generated by `presentation/build.py` from `artifacts/*.json`. Numbers update when the experiments are re-run.*

**[0:00 — Slide 1, question]**
The quantum-kernel SVM is the first QML example almost everyone runs, and it classifies breast-cancer data nicely. Our question: does it beat a classical model when the comparison is fair? And what would it cost on a real device?

**[0:15 — Slide 2, protocol]**
Every model sees exactly the same thing: 15 outer folds, and scaling plus PCA fitted on each training fold only. A test proves there is no leakage. An inner CV tunes every hyperparameter, including the quantum kernel's bandwidth. We compare the quantum kernel tuned and at the tutorial setting with an RBF SVM and logistic regression. Differences go through the Nadeau–Bengio corrected t-test, because CV folds overlap and the naive test is overconfident.

**[0:45 — Slide 3, results]**
Tuned, the quantum kernel beats the RBF SVM in 0 of 12 settings, across two datasets and 2 to 12 qubits. The gaps are small, −1.9 pts to −0.4 pts, a statistical tie, but it is never ahead. At the tutorial setting it collapses: breast-cancer accuracy falls from 89.5% to 66.0%. The best model on each dataset is a plain RBF SVM: 97.7% on breast cancer, 99.8% on wine. The quantum kernel's one nominal win is over logistic regression on wine at 2 qubits, one test out of 12.

**[1:20 — Slide 4, why]**
Why? At the tutorial setting, kernel values concentrate. Their spread shrinks about 2.7 times per qubit, and from 8 qubits a thousand shots can't resolve it, so every patient looks unrelated to every other. Cross-validation fixes this with a small bandwidth, median 0.05. But there, the geometric difference to an RBF kernel is only 1.2 to 3.1: a classical kernel already does the same job. Tuning rescues accuracy by making the kernel classical.

**[1:50 — Slide 5, hardware]**
On a device it gets harder. A thousand shots give kernel error around 0.01. The FakeTorino noise model, run locally, gives 0.27–0.31, about 25 times worse. And you need one circuit per pair of samples: 155,155 for a single CV fold.

**[2:10 — Slide 6, takeaways]**
So tune the bandwidth, check the geometric difference, and always run a tuned classical baseline on the same features and splits. Everything reruns in about three minutes, and every number on these slides is generated from the saved results. Classical simulation only, and no quantum advantage claimed. What we offer is a reusable, honest test bench for the next quantum-kernel idea. Thank you.
